name: Battle of Nagashino
info: In June 1575 the allied armies of Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated Takeda Katsuyori's army near Nagashino Castle in Mikawa Province, Japan, killing many Takeda generals and making Nobunaga's unification of Japan seem certain.

facts.date: June 1575: the siege of Nagashino Castle began that month, the armies faced each other on 28 June and the main battle was fought on 29 June, from early morning until about 2 pm according to the Shinchō Kōki
facts.place: Nagashino Castle and Shitaragahara, about 4 km to its west, in Mikawa Province (present-day Shinshiro, Aichi Prefecture, Japan)
facts.sides: Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu, with 38,000 men by the usual figure (about 30,000 Oda and about 8,000 Tokugawa troops); Takeda Katsuyori, with 15,000, of whom 12,000 marched to the main battle and 3,000 stayed at the siege
facts.outcome: The Oda-Tokugawa forces won, and the Takeda army lost many of its commanders; the Shinchō Kōki puts Takeda losses at 10,000 men. Katsuyori withdrew to Kai Province.

t: The Takeda army of about 15,000 faced an Oda-Tokugawa force put at 38,000, and recent research stresses the allied superiority in troops and firepower over any new tactic.
The familiar story of Nobunaga's three volleys fired in turn by 3,000 guns comes from later war tales and a 1903 military history; the Shinchō Kōki mentions about 1,000 guns and no volleys in turn.
Many Takeda commanders died, but according to recent research most of them were killed during the retreat, and the Takeda clan lasted until 1582.
dyk: Torii Suneemon, sent out of besieged Nagashino Castle to ask Ieyasu for reinforcements, was captured on his way back; offered his life if he called out that no help was coming, he shouted that help would certainly come, and he was crucified.
ev: Takeda Shingen falls ill during a campaign in Mikawa and the Takeda forces withdraw to Kai Province while concealing his death
Tokugawa forces under Honda Tadakatsu and Sakakibara Yasumasa take Nagashino Castle, and Takeda Katsuyori leads his main force into Okumikawa
Katsuyori besieges Nagashino Castle, held by 500 men, and Ieyasu asks Oda Nobunaga for help
Nobunaga leaves Gifu with about 30,000 men and joins Ieyasu at Okazaki the next day
Nobunaga halts at Shitaragahara and the allies build fences and earthworks
Katsuyori marches east of Shitaragahara with 12,000 men and the two armies face each other across the Rengo River
Sakai Tadatsugu's detachment attacks from behind Mount Tobigasu, and the Takeda army attacks the allied lines and is routed
The Takeda clan is destroyed, seven years after Nagashino

sections.background:
The trigger was the contest between Tokugawa Ieyasu and Takeda Katsuyori over North Mikawa. The Takeda and Tokugawa clans had been at war since the lifetime of Takeda Shingen. The Takeda forces were overwhelmingly superior in strength, and the Okudaira clan and other provincial leaders of Okumikawa in the north-east of Mikawa joined the Takeda side to prolong their lives. Ieyasu had a powerful ally in Oda Nobunaga, who held the capital and was rapidly increasing his power, but Nobunaga was by no means an equal ally, and used Ieyasu as a bulwark against the Takeda.

When Shingen fell ill during a campaign in Mikawa in May 1573, the Takeda forces retreated to Kai Province and worked to transfer power to Katsuyori while concealing Shingen's death. Ieyasu, sensing something unusual in their movements, set out to reverse the situation and manoeuvred the kunishū, the powerful families of Okumikawa, to regain the north of Mikawa. His forces sent Honda Tadakatsu and Sakakibara Yasumasa to take Nagashino Castle, which gave Ieyasu a strategic transport point and a base in the region.

Katsuyori, having finished his succession, led the main force of the Takeda army into Okumikawa. He moved south along the Toyokawa River and ravaged the whole of East Mikawa, launching raids throughout the estates of the Tokugawa vassals.
sections.forces:
The allied forces of Nobunaga and Ieyasu are put at 38,000 and Katsuyori's at 15,000. Katsuyori besieged Nagashino Castle, which had only 500 defenders, with 15,000 men. Ieyasu could mobilise only about 8,000 troops, and Nobunaga came with an Oda force of about 30,000 and his heir, Oda Nobutada. On 28 June Katsuyori marched to the east of Shitaragahara with a main force of 12,000 and left 3,000 men at the siege.

Nobunaga made his main camp on Mount Gokurakuji, west of Shitaragahara, and Nobutada camped on Mount Shinmido. Ieyasu camped on Mount Takamatsu, facing the Rengo River. Shitaragahara is a depression, and Nobunaga placed his 30,000 men so that they did not look like a large force from the Takeda side. The Shinchō Kōki says the allies steadily built positions with horse defence fences and earthworks.

The Shinchō Kōki records that Nobunaga deployed about 1,000 matchlock guns between five commanders, Sassa Narimasa, Maeda Toshiie, Nonomura Masanari, Fukuzumi Hidekatsu and Ban Naomasa. Some manuscripts read 3,000, and it is unclear who changed the number. A further 500 guns went with Sakai Tadatsugu's detachment. Takeda military registers show that the Takeda army also held about 1,000 to 1,500 guns. Neither army had units made up wholly of horsemen: vassals brought cavalry, spearmen and archers according to their lands and wealth, and these fought in groups.
sections.course:
In June 1575 Katsuyori invaded Mikawa and surrounded Nagashino Castle. Ieyasu asked Nobunaga for help, and Nobunaga left Gifu on 21 June and joined Ieyasu at Okazaki on 22 June. Torii Suneemon was sent out of the castle to Okazaki to ask for reinforcements. On his way back with the news that help was coming he was captured, and was promised his life and a reward if he shouted to the castle that no help would come. He shouted that reinforcements would certainly come and was crucified.

Nobunaga reached Shitaragahara on 26 June and halted instead of relieving the castle. Katsuyori's vassals advised him to retreat to Kai, but he judged the enemy weak, since the allies did not come to the castle's relief and were fortifying, and he decided to fight. After the armies faced each other across the Rengo River, Nobunaga took up a suggestion from the Tokugawa vassal Sakai Tadatsugu. Sakai set out at night with a column of about 4,000 men and early on 29 June attacked the Takeda troops from behind Mount Tobigasu. The detachment joined the men of Nagashino Castle and drove the Takeda forces off.

With its retreat cut off, the main Takeda army charged the Oda and Tokugawa camps in front of it one after another. Nobunaga came to Ieyasu's camp on Mount Takamatsu and took command, sending a matchlock corps under five bugyō to the front. Repeated Takeda charges were stopped by the guns and fences, and by midday the Takeda forces were routed. The Shinchō Kōki says the battle lasted until about 2 pm, and that Nobunaga pressed the retreating Takeda and inflicted further casualties.
sections.aftermath:
According to the Shinchō Kōki the Takeda lost 10,000 men, two-thirds of the force that had besieged the castle. Several of the Twenty-Four Generals of Takeda Shingen died, among them Baba Nobuharu, Hara Masatane, Sanada Nobutsuna and his younger brother Sanada Masateru, Yamagata Masakage, Saegusa Moritomo, Tsuchiya Masatsugu, Naitō Masatoyo and Obata Masamori. Yamagata Masakage was killed by a gunshot. Recent research holds that most of the Takeda commanders died during the retreat and not in the fighting.

Katsuyori could no longer afford to conquer other territories and withdrew to his stronghold in Kai. In early July, immediately after the victory, Ieyasu led his army to retake one castle after another that the Takeda had captured. Katsuyori remained a stubborn opponent and went on troubling Ieyasu by regrouping as he retreated. In 1577 a Takeda general, Miura Uemonnosuke, tried to take Hōkizuka Castle and failed against the Tokugawa general Abe Motozane.

Katsuyori instructed his troops to prepare 200 to 300 rounds of ammunition per gun after the battle. The Takeda clan was not destroyed until 1582, seven years after the defeat at Nagashino and Shitaragahara.
sections.sources:
The Shinchō Kōki is the chief account and is regarded as highly reliable. It gives the strength of the gun corps as 1,000, the five commanders, the length of the battle and the Takeda losses, and it does not mention volleys fired in turn. The Mikawa Monogatari, written by Ōkubo Tadataka, a vassal of Ieyasu, does not even give the number of guns. The tale of three-stage shooting comes from the Shinchōki, a war tale written by the Edo-period Confucian scholar Oze Hoan, and was carried into Nihon Senshi Nagashino no Eki, a history compiled by the Imperial Japanese Army General Staff Office in 1903. Tokutomi Sohō's Kinsei Nihon Kokuminshi (1918 to 1952) followed that account entirely.

Doubts about the volleys were first voiced by the amateur researcher Fujimoto Masayuki in his 1980 essay Nagashino no Teppō Senjutsu wa Kyokō da, and the prevailing view now is that three-stage shooting by 3,000 guns was a later invention. Research in the 2010s added new findings and interpretations. Scientific analysis of shot found on the battlefield shows that the lead in the allied shot was of three types, domestic, South Chinese and Korean, and Thai, while the Takeda shot is nearly identical in composition to imported Chinese coins, suggesting that it was made by melting copper coins.
sections.legacy:
The battle is often cited as a turning point in Japanese warfare and as the first modern battle in Japan, and after it Nobunaga's unification of the country was seen as certain. It came to be remembered as the battle in which Katsuyori recklessly drove his cavalry against long horse defence fences where Nobunaga waited with 3,000 matchlock guns. A myth grew that Nobunaga was a military genius who devised three-stage shooting, and the scene has been depicted repeatedly in films, television dramas and other fiction. The historical community at the time of Sohō held a similar view, which lasted long after the Second World War.

Recent research has overturned this belief, and Katsuyori is being re-evaluated. The allied victory is attributed to their superiority in firepower and troop numbers, Nobunaga's placing of his forces, and the Takeda misjudging their opponents' strength and attacking head on. Charging at the enemy line was common in battles of the time, and the term Takeda cavalry is inappropriate. The Takeda had promoted guns since Shingen's time but found lead, nitrates and guns hard to obtain, while Nobunaga controlled the port of Sakai and the Kyoto and Kinai trade and bought materials from overseas. Recent writing calls the battle one between the Oda, with abundant supplies in the west, and the Takeda, who lacked them in the east. The battle is now often named the Battle of Nagashino and Shitaragahara, after the castle and the place where the final fighting took place.

summary: In June 1575 Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated Takeda Katsuyori near Nagashino Castle in Mikawa, killing many Takeda generals. The familiar tale of volleys fired in turn by 3,000 guns is now thought a later invention, and recent research stresses allied numbers, firepower and supplies.
notes: Strengths: the lead says 38,000 allied against 15,000 Takeda; the siege section gives about 30,000 Oda and about 8,000 Tokugawa (which sum to 38,000, but I give them as the article gives them) and Katsuyori's 15,000 at the castle, yet on 28 June his main force was 12,000 with 3,000 left at the siege. Both are given.

Guns: 1,000 (Shinchō Kōki), 3,000 (later manuscripts and tradition), 500 with Sakai, 'at least 1,500' in total inferred by the article; Takeda 1,000-1,500. The article's 'at least 1,500' is not stated in my text.

The article's 'Nobunaga adopted a suggestion from Sakai Tadatsugu ... Tobigasu' passage is muddled: it speaks of a fort held by the Takeda behind Mount Tobigasu and of the detachment entering the castle. I kept it close to the article's wording.

Left out as garbled or inconsistent: the sentence on Tadakatsu capturing Komyo castle in June (no year context, separate campaign); the 'Fukutomi Hidekatsu' / 'Fukuzumi Hidekatsu' and 'Nonomura Masashige' / 'Masanari' spelling variants between the text and the commanders list (I used the Analysis spellings); the paragraph on Tatsuo Fujita's view that the battle showed Portuguese ambitions to make Japan a colony (an idiosyncratic claim, poorly written); and the commanders lists.

The article gives the date only as 'June 1575' in the lead and Battle section, with 28 and 29 June for the main battle; the Shinchō Kōki is cited for 'about 2 pm'. It also says Nobunaga 'left Gifu on 21 June' and 'reached Shitaragahara 26 June'. Not given: the Japanese lunar-calendar date.
The 10,000 Takeda dead is 'two-thirds of his original besieging force' (15,000) by the article; I gave it as the Shinchō Kōki's figure with that comparison.
The article's lead calls the victory 'crushing'; I avoided the word. 'Decisive battle' appears in the article only for Katsuyori's choice to fight.
